note: Refreshed every week by the program's research task. Each item says what changed, why it matters to a data engineer or architect, and how to test the claim yourself.

items.title: Claude API: message threads keep the conversation on the server, so each turn sends only the new messages (beta)
items.summary: Released on 2 November 2026 in beta behind the message-threads-2026-08-12 header. The Messages API can keep a conversation on Anthropic's side; later requests send only the new messages. A thread expires 5 minutes after its last request and is deleted no more than an hour after last use. Available on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, Claude models on Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry.
items.why: An agent loop resends its whole history every turn, so request size and latency grow with every tool call. Server-side threads shrink the payload, but the 5-minute expiry means a long-running agent still needs its own durable record of the run, the same split between hot state and a log you design for any pipeline.
items.try: In projects/ai-foundations/labs/lab1_loop.py, log the request size in bytes per turn for a 10-turn run. Write down how the curve would change with server-side threads, and what your harness must persist itself so a run that pauses longer than 5 minutes can resume.

items.title: Claude Console: IP allowlisting limits where a leaked API key works (beta)
items.summary: Released on 5 November 2026 in beta. An organization can list up to 1,000 IPv4 or IPv6 addresses or CIDR ranges; API requests from anywhere else are refused. The same release lets the Admin API sign an Enterprise member out of Claude everywhere while keeping them in the organization.
items.why: Agents and pipelines hold long-lived API keys on schedulers and CI runners. An allowlist turns a leaked key from 'usable from anywhere' into 'usable only from our egress IPs', the same network control you already put on a warehouse or a database.
items.try: For the on-call agent in lab10_oncall.py, list every place its API key lives (laptop, CI, scheduler) and the egress IP of each. Decide which ranges go on the allowlist and what breaks first when a runner's IP changes.

items.title: Snowflake: background agents with an Async Agent API and scheduled CoCo Automations (GA), bots in preview
items.summary: Announced at Snowflake Expedition 2026 on 3 November 2026. CoCo Automations and the Async Agent API for scheduled and long-running agent work are generally available, as is sharing of skills and plugins. CoCo and CoWork Bots, always-on agents that act with the user's own access rights and check in only for decisions or sign-off, are coming in private preview.
items.why: Long-running agents move from a chat window to a job you schedule, monitor and pay for like any pipeline. Acting with the user's rights keeps governance in the warehouse's roles, but it also means an agent can do anything its owner can, so the sign-off points are the guardrail.
items.try: Turn lab10_oncall.py into an asynchronous job: start it, return a run id at once, poll for the result. Write down which steps need a human sign-off and what the agent may do without one.

items.title: Snowflake: self-healing pipelines trace a failure's likely cause and propose a fix for an engineer to review
items.summary: Announced on 5 November 2026 at Snowflake Expedition. Scheduled runs of Snowflake's coding agent trace the likely cause of a pipeline failure and propose a fix for an engineer's review; the agent can run in a Snowflake-managed isolated container after you log off. Snowflake also announced a visual Pipeline Builder and Write-Audit-Publish on Iceberg tables.
items.why: This is the on-call data agent you build in A3.5, now a vendor feature. The design questions stay yours: what evidence the agent must cite, which actions need approval, and how you score it on failures you injected yourself.
items.try: Run lab11_eval.py against your on-call agent, then score a 'propose only, never apply' version on the same 10 injected failures. Compare correct cause, unsafe actions and cost per incident.

items.title: Snowflake Cortex AI Gateway: automatic model tiers route each request to a model (private preview)
items.summary: Announced on 3 November 2026. Auto model tiers with dynamic model routing for Snowflake's coding agent, part of Cortex AI Gateway, are in private preview. Cortex Training, serverless reinforcement learning and fine-tuning of open-weight models, is in public preview; Snowflake claims up to 61% lower cost than existing serverless training options.
items.why: Routing cheap requests to a small model is the biggest cost lever after caching, and it is moving into the platform gateway. A router is only as good as the eval that says the cheap tier holds up for your tasks.
items.try: In lab7_optimise.py, route each task to a small or a large model by a simple rule (input length or task type). Run lab5_evals.py on both and report pass rate and cost per passed task for routed versus always-large.

items.title: Snowflake Datastream: Kafka-compatible ingestion with no brokers to run, and Snowpipe Streaming up to 20 GB a second
items.summary: Announced on 5 November 2026. Snowflake Datastream accepts Kafka-protocol producers with no brokers or connectors to manage. Snowpipe Streaming with Elastic Channels reaches up to 20 GB a second with data ready in a median of three seconds; Streaming Transformations apply SQL to data in motion, and Interactive Analytics targets sub-second queries for apps and agents.
items.why: Fresh features and context for agents usually means a Kafka cluster plus a connector. A Kafka-compatible endpoint inside the warehouse removes that hop, but you give up the topic as a shared, replayable log for other consumers, which is a trade-off to name in a design interview.
items.try: Using the 5.9 lens table, compare a Kafka cluster with Connect into the warehouse against a Kafka-compatible warehouse endpoint for one agent's feature feed: who can replay, who else can consume, and what each costs at 50 MB a second.
